chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: His sister keeps Fletcher's papers and records in Georgia; cataloguing plan
summary: After Fletcher and his wife died, the 139th Street house was sold and papers and experimental discs were moved to Horace's sister in Georgia. The interviewer offers to help catalogue them.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Hunting for old band photographs and scrapbooks

blocks.x: Yeah, uh-huh. I see. So did you ever keep any -- like sketch pads or anything like that that you used?

Yes, I probably did that sometimes because a lot of times you would try to remember not to repeat, you know, certain things, you know, and it was essential that I did do that. You know, I've got a lot of that stuff, Tom, at my sister's home in Georgia now, you know, because when Fletcher passed and his wife passed -- I used to keep a lot of stuff in New York. Of course, they left their home to us in New York, 228 West 139th Street, and when that was sold, we decided to sell it rather, and when it was sold and we moved a lot of that stuff to where I knew it wouldn't be sold, you know. My sister's -- she treasures all that stuff. And I've got a lot of valuable stuff down there. This is one of the reasons why I'm contemplating on taking a little trip,

you know. And I don't know. I would actually like to drive if I had the time, so I could bring stuff back, you know. And a lot of records, and you know we used to cut a lot of those little discs, you know, little records in those days, you know, little experimental things.
Right.

And they were real good, you know. We used to do that even when the guys in the band didn't know that that was happening, you know? And you used to hear some talking, conversation, all those things, and some classics on (unintelligible) there.
(Laughter)
I'll bet there are.

So they're there, and, of course, my sister is well aware of how important that is, and she doesn't let anybody touch those things. This is one of my anxious reasons on this for wanting to go down there.
Uh-huh. You know, sometime for history's sake and so on, it might be worthwhile, if you really wanted to get into it, to get somebody to help you with that and catalog it, organize it and --
Be nice to compile it, wouldn't it?
It really would, I think.
Well, a guy named Tom should be all right on that.
Well, I wasn't hinting or anything,
but just let me know.
(Laughter)
Well, that's beautiful, because it would be interesting, you know, of the things that would be discovered. Just like an easter egg hunt.
Uh-huh. I think it would be especially interesting for you because, you know, everything you're going to pick up is going to be, "Oh, yeah, I remember that."
Yeah, you Always remember the incident after you've run across that thing, you know. Take you a couple of minutes on some of them, but they come back to you.
Well, seriously, you know, if you ever think about it, I'd be very willing to help you.
That's really nice to know. Because well, this is one of the things that I've often wanted to do, but I've just been so busy, you know. When you work like we are now.
Oh, I know, playing six nights a week.

(Unintelligible). It's a rough thing. You don't have time to travel that far. Going by plane, you might as well not go; if you're going to bring that stuff back, you won't get back, financially, you know. Plus the fact that it's heavy.
